question: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE) Subject:

Food and parcel delivery services via digital platforms such as Uber Eats and Deliveroo have become widespread in Europe’s big cities. However, a number of studies point to worrying abuses: most of the delivery workers are immigrants, who are often working on an insecure or irregular basis, exploited and exposed to significant health risks. This raises social and economic questions. At the same time, this work, which was originally done by students or active young Europeans, including cyclists, could be a lever for getting young Europeans into the labour market, while also contributing to the EU’s climate objectives. 1.

Does the Commission intend to promote a European workforce in this sector, while respecting the competences of the Member States, through programmes focusing on soft mobility, sport and youth employment?

Does the Commission plan to incorporate these issues into policies on youth, sport and the green transition, in order to promote these urban cycling-related jobs as a way to boost local and sustainable employment?
Finally, could it encourage the exchange of good practices on social and health-related conditions in order to combat economic exploitation in this sector?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.6.2026) Directive (EU) 2024/28311 aims to improve working conditions in platform work and to support the opportunities the platform economy offers, including for young people. Its provisions on transparency, intermediaries and reliable identity verification, together with the minimum standards on sanctions and measures against employers of illegally staying third-country nationals set out by Directive 2009/52/EC2 should strongly contribute to address undeclared work and other illegal practices involving undocumented migrants in the delivery sector3,4. The Commission supports the sharing of good practices via its mutual learning programme. Moreover, the European Labour Authority has organised several events and published relevant reports reflecting enforcement challenges and approaches at national level, addressing in particular employment status misclassification and undeclared work in the platform economy5. The Commission’s efforts in the area of platform work are in synergy with its policies to foster quality jobs, sustainable modes of transport and health-enhancing physical activity within the green and digital transitions. The reinforced Youth Guarantee6 remains pivotal and has already enabled 63 million young Europeans to start an offer of employment, continued education, apprenticeships and traineeships, including in the green economy
